title: MuscleClear
question: How do your muscles move you?
hook: More than 600 muscles, a third of your body, and every one can only pull. Peel a body down to its muscles, zoom into a sarcomere to watch myosin heads tug on actin with ATP, work out how hard your biceps pulls, and race the three energy systems.

explainer.title: More than 600 motors under your skin
explainer.text: Skeletal muscles are about a third of your body mass, joined to bones by tendons: the deltoid, biceps and triceps, pectorals and abs, glutes, quadriceps, hamstrings and calves. The diaphragm, a dome under the lungs, does most of your breathing.

explainer.title: Three kinds of muscle
explainer.text: Skeletal muscle is striped and voluntary. Cardiac muscle is striped, branched and runs on its own pacemaker, beating about a lakh times a day without tiring. Smooth muscle in the gut and vessels has no stripes and squeezes slowly for seconds.

explainer.title: Millions of tiny tugs
explainer.text: A muscle is bundles of fibres, fibres are packed with myofibrils, and myofibrils are chains of 2.5 µm sarcomeres. A nerve signal releases calcium, myosin heads grab actin and pull, one ATP per stroke, and the filaments slide so each sarcomere shortens to about 2.0 µm.

explainer.title: Muscles only pull
explainer.text: So they work in opposing pairs: biceps and triceps, quadriceps and hamstrings. The biceps grips the forearm about 5 cm from the elbow while your hand is 33 cm away, so it pulls about seven times the weight you hold.

explainer.title: Fuel, fibres and fatigue
explainer.text: Phosphocreatine lasts about 10 s, glycolysis a minute or two, and aerobic respiration for hours. Sprinters are mostly fast-twitch, marathoners mostly slow-twitch. Lactate doesn't cause next-day soreness, and training thickens fibres rather than adding new ones.

explainer.title: Keeping them strong
explainer.text: Strains usually heal with rest; see a doctor for a pop or if you can't walk. After 30, muscle falls about 3–8% a decade, but strength training twice a week (WHO) and enough protein help at any age.

concepts.def: Striped, voluntary muscle joined to bones by tendons.
A tough cord of collagen that joins a muscle to a bone.
The repeating unit of a muscle fibre, about 2–2.5 µm long, from one Z-disc to the next.
The thin and thick filaments; myosin heads pull on actin to make the filaments slide.
Grab, pull, release, re-cock: one ATP per stroke for each myosin head.
Two muscles that pull a joint opposite ways, like biceps and triceps.
The energy molecule every muscle stroke spends, remade by phosphocreatine, glycolysis and aerobic respiration.
Type I fibres are steady and tireless; type II are quick and powerful but tire fast.
Loss of muscle mass and strength with age.
